newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian lawmakers turn fire on Yeltsin aide.
newsitem.headline: Russian lawmakers turn fire on Yeltsin aide.

text.p: A Kremlin aide under fire in the upper house of the Russian parliament shrugged off calls to oust him on Thursday and said only President Boris Yeltsin, who is recovering from pneumonia, could force him out of office.

Businessman Boris Berezovsky, criticised by parliament for suggesting that Cossacks in southern Russia should be allowed to bear arms in self-defence, told Ekho Moskvy radio that parliament's suggestion was senseless.
"It is for the president to decide," he said.
Interfax news agency had said the Federation Council had called on Yeltsin to sack Berezovsky, but it later said these paragraphs were deleted from the final resolution.
But the council warned that any militarisation in the volatile north Caucasus region could lead to new bloodshed.

"If we arm the civilian population, there could without a doubt be a second Caucasus war and the Federation Council is decisively against that, but not against individuals," Interfax quoted council head Yegor Stroyev as saying.
Yeltsin is already under attack in the lower house of parliament, where deputies on Wednesday debated a motion urging him out of office on health grounds.
Deputies also want to investigate presidential chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais on allegations of tax evasion. Chubais denies the charges.
Aides say the president, 65, returned briefly to the Kremlin on Wednesday, two days after completing a hospital course of treatment for double pneumonia.

Russian television showed pictures -- from a distance -- of a black limousine pulling up outside the main Kremlin building on Wednesday but, in contrast to the practice after previous illnesses, there were no pictures of Yeltsin himself.

Doctors, warning him not to race back to work, say he will need another two or three weeks to recover, although Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Thursday that he expected Yeltsin to be back at work within days.
The presidential press service said Yeltsin was working on documents at a country residence on Thursday.
Yeltsin spent most of the second half of 1996 getting ready for heart surgery and then recovering from a bypass operation and his political foes say he is not well enough to rule Russia.

Yeltsin's absences, criticism of his aides and parliament's attempts to censure him have increased the impression of a rudderless country and boosted speculation that Yeltsin might not see out his four-year term in office.
"It seems nobody has reliable information about the president's condition and the extent of his work capacity today," said the liberal newspaper Sevodnya.
Yeltsin was elected last July for a second term which is due to end in the year 2000.

If an election were held early, candidates would probably include one-time security chief Alexander Lebed, Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky and Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov.
Many political analysts say Lebed would be the most likely victor if the election were held soon.
